evidence_passages.text:
**Supported Facts**

- In the primary BM25 paper, Robertson and Walker say their goal is to use the 2-Poisson model to incorporate three variables into probabilistic retrieval weighting: within-document term frequency, document length, and within-query term frequency. They also report that the resulting simple weighting functions produced “considerable performance improvements” over simple inverse collection-frequency weighting on TREC. Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4471-2099-5_24

- In a later author-written technical note, Robertson and Sparck Jones describe BM25 as a formula for combining three kinds of per-term evidence into a request-document matching score: collection frequency weight, within-document term frequency, and document length; document scores are then the sum of the query-term weights present in the document, and documents are ranked by descending score. Source: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf

- That same technical note defines the three core evidence sources explicitly:
  `CFW(i) = log N - log n` for collection frequency / inverse document frequency style weighting; `TF(i,j)` as the number of occurrences of term `t(i)` in document `d(j)`; and normalized document length `NDL(j) = DL(j) / Average DL`. Source: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf

- The author-written TREC-4 paper gives a BM25 variant with these scoring factors: Robertson-Sparck Jones relevance weight `w(1)`, document term frequency `tf`, query term frequency `qtf`, and document-length normalization through `K = k1((1-b)+b*dl/avdl)`. It defines `tf`, `qtf`, `dl`, and `avdl` directly. Source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf

- The TREC-6 paper by the same authors says the Okapi BM25 function was “first used in TREC-3.” Source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec6_auto.pdf

- The authors explicitly interpret `k1` as controll

runs.final_answer:
**Supported Facts**

- In the primary BM25 paper, Robertson and Walker say their goal is to use the 2-Poisson model to incorporate three variables into probabilistic retrieval weighting: within-document term frequency, document length, and within-query term frequency. They also report that the resulting simple weighting functions produced “considerable performance improvements” over simple inverse collection-frequency weighting on TREC. Source: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4471-2099-5_24

- In a later author-written technical note, Robertson and Sparck Jones describe BM25 as a formula for combining three kinds of per-term evidence into a request-document matching score: collection frequency weight, within-document term frequency, and document length; document scores are then the sum of the query-term weights present in the document, and documents are ranked by descending score. Source: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf

- That same technical note defines the three core evidence sources explicitly:
  `CFW(i) = log N - log n` for collection frequency / inverse document frequency style weighting; `TF(i,j)` as the number of occurrences of term `t(i)` in document `d(j)`; and normalized document length `NDL(j) = DL(j) / Average DL`. Source: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf

- The author-written TREC-4 paper gives a BM25 variant with these scoring factors: Robertson-Sparck Jones relevance weight `w(1)`, document term frequency `tf`, query term frequency `qtf`, and document-length normalization through `K = k1((1-b)+b*dl/avdl)`. It defines `tf`, `qtf`, `dl`, and `avdl` directly. Source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf

- The TREC-6 paper by the same authors says the Okapi BM25 function was “first used in TREC-3.” Source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec6_auto.pdf

- The authors explicitly interpret `k1` as controlling the influence of within-document term frequency: higher `k1` increases TF influence, and `k1=0` removes TF influence. Source: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf

- The authors explicitly interpret `b` as controlling document-length normalization, with `b` ranging from 0 to 1. They say `b=1` corresponds to the assumption that long documents are long because they are repetitive, while `b=0` corresponds to the assumption that long documents are long because they are multi-topic. They further say that moving `b` toward 1 reduces TF’s effect on the view that extra length is mostly verbosity, and they report that `b=.75` was helpful in TREC. Source: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf

- The authors report a practical interpretation of `k3` through query-term repetition: in TREC-4, terms occurring more than once in the topic statement were given a bonus by setting `k3 = 8`; the same paper lists typical TREC-4 values `k1` in `1.0-2.0`, `k3 = 8`, `b` in `0.6-0.75`, and `k2 = 0` throughout. Source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf

**Inference**

- The best-supported answer to “what problem does BM25 solve?” is: BM25 is a probabilistic ranking function for document retrieval that was introduced to improve on simpler weighting schemes by combining term rarity with within-document term frequency, document length normalization, and sometimes within-query term frequency. This is an inference from the authors’ statements about the variables added, the ranking use, and the reported improvement over simple inverse collection-frequency weighting. Sources: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4471-2099-5_24 ; https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec6_auto.pdf

**Disagreement / Uncertainty**

- There is no strong disagreement in the primary sources I found about the main factors: all accessible author sources consistently point to term rarity / relevance weight, document TF, and document length normalization; TREC-era BM25 variants also include query term frequency `qtf`. Sources: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf

- There is some uncertainty about whether `qtf` should be treated as part of “core BM25” in the narrowest sense, because the Cambridge technical note presents a simplified BM25 form with `K1` and `b`, while the TREC-4/TREC-6 Okapi BM25 formula also includes `k3` and `qtf`. Both are author sources, so the safest reading is that `qtf` is part of at least some primary Okapi BM25 formulations, but not always present in simplified presentations. Sources: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec6_auto.pdf

**Lack of Good Evidence**

- I found clear author-supported interpretations for `k1`, `b`, and the practical use of `k3`, but not a comparably clear author explanation of the semantic role of `k2` in the accessible primary pages I could open. What is directly supported is only that `k2` appears in the TREC-4/TREC-6 formula and was set to zero in TREC-4. Sources: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec6_auto.pdf

**Short Answer**

- Problem solved: probabilistic document ranking with better weighting than simple inverse collection frequency, by incorporating TF, length normalization, and in some primary Okapi formulations query TF. Sources: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4471-2099-5_24 ; https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf

- Core scoring factors: term rarity / RSJ relevance weight, within-document term frequency, document length normalization, and sometimes within-query term frequency. Sources: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf

- Supported parameter interpretations: `k1` controls TF saturation strength; `b` controls the length-normalization assumption from multi-topic (`b=0`) to verbosity/repetition (`b=1`); `k3` controls the bonus for repeated query terms; good primary evidence for `k2`’s interpretation was not found in the accessible sources. Sources: https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/techreports/UCAM-CL-TR-356.pdf ; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/okapi_trec4.pdf

# Problem Addressed

This paper tackles the challenge of incorporating multiple variables into probabilistic information retrieval models. Rather than choosing between rigid formal models and ad-hoc approaches, the authors seek "a model which provides an exact but intractable formula, and use it to suggest a much simpler formula."

The three key variables examined are: within-document term frequency (tf), document length (d), and within-query term frequency (qtf).

---

# 2-Poisson Model and Eliteness Motivation

The foundation rests on the **eliteness hypothesis**: documents either are or aren't "about" a query concept, creating a hidden distinction that affects term occurrence patterns. "Relevance (to a query which may of course contain many concepts) is related to eliteness rather than directly to term frequency."

The 2-Poisson model assumes elite documents exhibit one Poisson distribution for term frequencies, while non-elite documents follow a different Poisson distribution—modeling how term occurrence reflects underlying topicality rather than randomness.

---

# BM11 and BM15 Formulas

**BM15** (Equation 8) applies term frequency without explicit document length normalization:

$$w = \frac{tf}{(k_1 + tf)} \times w^{(1)}$$

**BM11** (Equation 10) incorporates document length normalization:

$$w = \frac{tf}{(k_1 \times d/\Delta + tf)} \times w^{(1)}$$

Both formulas multiply an inverse collection frequency weight $w^{(1)}$ by a dampened term frequency component.

---

# Parameter Roles

**k₁**: Controls the "saturation point" where tf impact plateaus. Testing revealed "values around 1–2 seem to be about right for the TREC data," with performance improving sharply from zero to approximately 2, then degrading gradually.

**k₂**: A document length correction factor (Equation 13):
$$\text{correction} = k_2 \times \frac{n_q(\Delta - d)}{(\Delta + d)}$$

This factor adjusts for document length independent of the tf component, with "small positive values" improving r

# BM25 Framework: Key Components and Caveats

## (a) BM25 Formula and Parameter Definitions

The classic BM25 term-weighting function is:

"wBM25_i(tf) = tf′/(k1 + tf′) × wRSJ_i"

where:

"tf′ = tf / B" and "B := ((1 − b) + b × dl/avdl), 0 ≤ b ≤ 1"

The complete formulation combines this saturation function with the RSJ weight component across query terms.

## (b) Interpretation of b Parameter and Normalization Hypotheses

The authors state: "setting b = 1 will perform full document-length normalisation, while b = 0 will switch normalisation off."

Regarding document length variation, they describe two competing explanations:

"Verbosity: Some authors are simply more verbose than others, using more words to say the same thing. Scope: Some authors have more to say: they may write a single document containing or covering more ground."

They conclude: "we suppose in general a combination: that each hypothesis represents some partial explanation."

## (c) Recommended Parameter Values

"in general values such as 0.5 < b < 0.8 and 1.2 < k1 < 2 are reasonably good in many circumstances."

However: "there is also evidence that optimal values do depend on other factors (such as the type of documents or queries)."

## (d) Eliteness and 2-Poisson Motivation

The authors introduce "a hidden property which we refer to as eliteness. This can be interpreted as a form of aboutness."

The model assumes: "tf is distributed as a mixture of two Poisson distributions — so that this model is known as the 2-Poisson model."

## (e) Theoretical Caveats and Approximations

The authors acknowledge several limitations:

**On the saturation function**: "the authors of BM25 decided to fit a simple parametric curve to this shape" rather than deriving it from first principles.

**On the 2-Poisson assumptions**: 
- "The model depends fairly crucially on the notion that all documents are of the same (fixed) length."
- "There is no attempt to normalise the probabilities across the full unigram model.

## Réponse (sources primaires : Robertson & Walker 1994 ; Robertson & Zaragoza 2009)

**Avertissement méthodologique préalable :** les deux textes primaires ne sont disponibles qu'en PDF ; l'extraction directe a échoué et j'ai dû passer par un proxy de conversion texte (`r.jina.ai`) sur les copies déposées par l'auteur lui-même sur son site à City, University of London. Les « citations » ci-dessous sont donc restituées via une chaîne d'extraction automatique : leur substance est fiable, leur ponctuation exacte ne l'est pas nécessairement. Je signale explicitement plus bas les points où cela crée une incertitude réelle.

### 1. Quel problème BM25 résout-il ?

**Fait étayé.** Le cadre est celui du *Probability Ranking Principle* : « If retrieved documents are ordered by decreasing probability of relevance on the data available, then the system's effectiveness is the best that can be obtained for the data » ([Robertson & Zaragoza, *The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond*](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf)). Le problème concret est donc : **classer les documents par probabilité de pertinence estimée**, alors que la pertinence réelle est inconnue. BM25 y répond comme « a term-weighting and document-scoring function » (même source).

**Fait étayé.** Le problème plus précis attaqué en 1994 est l'**intégration de trois variables** que les modèles probabilistes antérieurs (à termes binaires) ignoraient : fréquence du terme dans le document (`tf`), longueur du document (`dl`), fréquence du terme dans la requête (`qtf`) ([Robertson & Walker, SIGIR'94](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/robertson_walker_sigir94.pdf) ; résumé confirmé par la [notice IR Anthology](https://ir.webis.de/anthology/1994.sigirconf_conference-94.24/) et la [notice Springer](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4471-2099-5_24)).

**Fait étayé.** La démarche assumée est celle d'une **approximation d'un modèle exact mais inexploitable** : les auteurs partent « d'un modèle qui fournit une formule exacte mais intraitable » et s'en servent pour suggérer une formule beaucoup plus simple, le problème d'estimation (quatre paramètres par terme) rendant la fonction de pondération intraitable ([SIGIR'94](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/robertson_walker_sigir94.pdf)).

### 2. Facteurs de score fondamentaux

**Fait étayé.** La forme classique donnée par les auteurs eux-mêmes :

```
w_BM25(tf) = tf' / (k1 + tf') × w_RSJ ,  avec tf' = tf / B
B = (1 − b) + b × dl/avdl ,  0 ≤ b ≤ 1
```
([Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf))

Trois composantes :

1. **Poids de terme (RSJ / IDF).** `w_RSJ = log[(r+0.5)(N−R−n+r+0.5)] / [(n−r+0.5)(R−r+0.5)]`, avec `r` = documents pertinents connus contenant le terme, `R` = taille de l'ensemble pertinent, `n` = documents contenant le terme, `N` = taille de la collection. **En l'absence d'information de pertinence (R = r = 0)**, il se réduit à une approximation d'IDF : `w_IDF = log[(N − n + 0.5)/(n + 0.5)]` ([Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf) ; même poids déjà présent comme équation 3 dans [SIGIR'94](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/robertson_walker_sigir94.pdf)). Point souvent mal compris : **l'IDF n'est pas le composant premier du modèle, c'est le cas dégénéré du poids de pertinence.**
2. **Saturation de la fréquence du terme** via `tf/(k1+tf)` : « any one term's contribution to the document score cannot exceed a saturation point (the asymptotic limit), however frequently it occurs in the document » ([Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf)).
3. **Normalisation par la longueur du document** via `B` et `b`.

Un quatrième composant, **`qtf`**, figurait dans BM25 d'origine « for longer queries where a term might occur multiple times » ; modélisé au départ avec une saturation paramétrée par `k3`, mais « the saturation effect for qtf was unimportant, leading to a formula which was linear in qtf » ([Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf)) — ce que corroborent les expériences de 1994, où le cas limite `w = qtf × w⁽¹⁾` était le plus efficace, avec un gain rapporté d'environ 37 % sur les requêtes longues ([SIGIR'94](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/robertson_walker_sigir94.pdf)).

### 3. Interprétations des paramètres soutenues par les auteurs

| Paramètre | Interprétation **explicitement soutenue** | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `k1` | Contrôle le point de saturation de `tf` ; valeurs « autour de 1–2 » adaptées aux données TREC | [SIGIR'94](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/robertson_walker_sigir94.pdf) |
| `b` | « setting b = 1 will perform full document-length normalisation, while b = 0 will switch normalisation off » | [Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf) |
| Plages usuelles | « in general values such as 0.5 < b < 0.8 and 1.2 < k1 < 2 are reasonably good in many circumstances » — **assorti d'une réserve** : « there is also evidence that optimal values do depend on other factors (such as the type of documents or queries) » | [Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf) |

**Justification sémantique de `b` (soutenue par les auteurs).** Deux hypothèses concurrentes expliquent la variation de longueur : **Verbosity** (« Some authors are simply more verbose than others, using more words to say the same thing ») et **Scope** (« Some authors have more to say »). Les auteurs ne tranchent pas : « we suppose in general a combination: that each hypothesis represents some partial explanation » ([Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf)). C'est bien l'hypothèse de verbosité qui motive la normalisation par `dl/avdl` en 1994 ([SIGIR'94](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/robertson_walker_sigir94.pdf)).

**Justification probabiliste (éliteness / 2-Poisson).** « a hidden property which we refer to as eliteness. This can be interpreted as a form of aboutness » ; `tf` est alors « distributed as a mixture of two Poisson distributions » ([Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf)). En 1994 : « Relevance […] is related to eliteness rather than directly to term frequency » ([SIGIR'94](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/robertson_walker_sigir94.pdf)).

### 4. Réserves posées par les auteurs eux-mêmes (fait étayé, souvent omis)

Les auteurs **ne présentent pas BM25 comme dérivé du modèle** : « the authors of BM25 decided to fit a simple parametric curve to this shape » ; le modèle 2-Poisson « depends fairly crucially on the notion that all documents are of the same (fixed) length » ; et sur les paramètres libres : « the model provides no guidance on how these should be set. This may be regarded as a limitation of the model » ([Robertson & Zaragoza](https://www.staff.city.ac.uk/~sbrp622/papers/foundations_bm25_review.pdf)). Leur revendication est une combinaison de modélisation théorique et de « pragmatic parameterisation ».

### 5. Incertitudes et limites de cette recherche

- **Incertitude réelle sur la paternité exacte de la forme à paramètre `b`.** L'extraction du texte SIGIR'94 indique que ce papier présente **BM11** (normalisation complète, `k1·d/Δ`) et **BM15** (aucune normalisation), mais **pas** l'interpolation par `b`. La littérature secondaire attribue généralement l'introduction de « BM25 » (interpolation BM11↔BM15) au papier *Okapi at TREC-3* de Robertson, Walker et al., que je **n'ai pas pu ouvrir** (NIST ne le diffuse qu'en PostScript compressé ; les autres liens trouvés sont des notices : [Semantic Scholar](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Okapi-at-TREC-3-Robertson-Walker/d2071c1e4a6030dc0005dbfeefdd196a8b293e84), [Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/okapi-at-trec-3/)). **Je ne peux donc pas confirmer sur source primaire** que `b` interpole entre BM11 et BM15, ni les valeurs `k1=1.2, b=0.75` qu'on attribue couramment à TREC-3 : c'est un point non résolu ici, non une affirmation vérifiée.
- **Divergence apparente entre les deux sources** sur `k2` : le texte de 1994 introduit un `k2` de correction de longueur indépendante de `tf` (« small positive values » améliorant les modèles non normalisés), paramètre absent de la formule BM25 canonique de 2009. Ce n'est pas une contradiction, mais un abandon ultérieur.
- **Inférence, non fait :** l'idée répandue que `k1` « corrige la répétition de mots-clés » ou que `b=0.75` serait un optimum universel n'est **pas** soutenue par les auteurs ; ils affirment au contraire la dépendance au corpus.
- **Fiabilité des citations :** voir l'avertissement initial — traitez les guillemets comme des citations reconstituées, à revérifier sur le PDF original avant tout usage académique.
